messages.subject: Erase unwanted sound
messages.body_plain:
Hello,

I have lots of wav files containing bird calls. Some of the recordings have lots of unwanted noise at various frequencies. What are the best ways of erasing the unwanted noise whilst keeping the bird calls?

Many thanks
Ross

messages.subject: Re: [seewave] Erase unwanted sound
messages.body_plain:
Hi Ross,

A common strategy is to use the ffilter() function, which can be used as a high-pass (e.g. getting rid of traffic noise), low-pass (e.g. getting rid of high-pitched insect noise), or bandstop filter (e.g. if you had an annoying narrowband noise in the same frequency range as your calls of interest, you could chop it out and still retain some of the signal of interest).

best,
jesse

messages.subject: Using seewave for microphone calibration testing
messages.subject_clean: Using seewave for microphone calibration testing
messages.body_plain:
Dear SeeWave users,

I would like to test some ultrasonic microphones in terms of a number of factors such as their detection distance, sensitivity deterioration and orientation in relation to sound source. I plan to use a calibration tool which emits a sound at a set frequency of 40 kHz in this testing.

I plan to test the difference between recordings by comparing the power of the signal recorded at 40 kHz. Are there any functions in seewave that enable you to measure signal power at a defined frequency or within a defined frequency band? Or, are there better measures you would suggest to conduct this testing that can be calculated using seewave?

Many thanks in advance for your assistance,
Alison
messages.body_snippet:

messages.subject: Re: [seewave] Using seewave for microphone calibration testing
messages.subject_clean: [seewave] Using seewave for microphone calibration testing
messages.body_plain:
Off the top of my head (and not as an expert) I would suggest using the spec() function with the argument norm = FALSE (i.e. don't normalize the amplitude data). This provides a frequency spectrum of amplitude by frequency. If you don't normalize the data and if you use a calibration tool, I think you should be able to compare the 40 kHz amplitude peaks.

Alternatively you could filter to a narrow band around 40kHz and use env() to calculate the amplitude envelope, and then take the root-mean-square to get an average amplitude at 40kHz.

It depends also on whether you simply want to compare the microphones, or whether you want to have concrete statistics about each one (comparisons are much easier).

Good luck!

Steffi
Dr. Stefanie LaZerte
stefanie...@unbc.ca
http://steffi.ca/

messages.subject_clean: Autocorrelation from indices when looking at continuous recordings

Just wondering how you all have dealt with autocorrelation in continuous recordings when using indices?

Quick chart from one of my recordings, 45mins long in a river. ACI calculated on each minute with no overlap. We have the issue of minutes being related to the minutes prior.
I know we could increase the interval between the calculations, are there any other ways you have dealt with this issue?

Cheers,
Chris

messages.subject: Re: [seewave] install seewave on Mac
messages.body_plain:
Hi Gianni,

I suspect that the requirement for root may have to do with XCode rather than seewave proper. The C and Fortran compilers on Macs are part of the XCode package, and you need to agree to that package's license agreement before you can use the compilers.

I believe that if you search for xcode in spotlight, open it up, and agree to the licensing stuff, the seewave compile should run fine without root.

best,
jesse

Try this in your terminal

brew install fftw

and may be as well

brew install lbsndfile

Jerome
